title: Man charged in connection to bomb threat at Illinois ethanol plant
summary:
Andrew M Kozak, 41, pleaded not guilty to two charges in federal court after an explosive device was found at facility

A 41-year-old man has been charged in connection to last week’s bomb…

blocks.text: A 41-year-old man has been charged in connection to last week’s bomb threat at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois.

On Tuesday, the justice department charged Andrew M Kozak, 41, of Chillicothe, Illinois, with one count of transmitting a threat through interstate or foreign commerce to unlawfully damage or destroy the plant using fire and an explosive, as well as one count of making threatening interstate communications.

Kozak pleaded not guilty during his first appearance in federal court on Tuesday. According to his LinkedIn page, he has been working as a process trainee at the plant since February, where he describes his role as: “Learning how to operate an ethanol plant.”
According to authorities, Kozak allegedly emailed the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant in Peoria last Friday, claiming explosive devices had been placed at the facility.

The threat prompted a significant law enforcement response and forced thousands of residents in parts of Peoria and East Peoria to evacuate last Friday. A mandatory evacuation order was issued for anyone living or working within a 1-mile radius of the plant and remained in effect until last Saturday afternoon.

Authorities discovered an explosive device at the facility, which produces ethanol for fuel and alcohol, both highly flammable products. The riverfront plant spans an area roughly equivalent to 44.5 US football fields. The device did not detonate and no injuries were reported.
The Guardian has reached out to BioUrja Renewables for comment.

“Threats to public safety generate fear in our community and cause significant disruption to residents, who deserve to go about their days free of worry about impending violence,” Gregory M Gilmore, US attorney for the central district of Illinois, said.
“My office is committed to prosecuting these serious crimes. We are grateful to our federal and local law enforcement partners for their dedicated work in furtherance of community safety,” he added.

Christopher Amon, the ATF’s Chicago field division special agent in charge, said: “An arrest was made in this case within 72 hours, demonstrating the tireless efforts of the law enforcement and intelligence personnel who worked around the clock to investigate an act that caused mass disruption and threatened the safety of the Peoria community.”

If convicted, Kozak faces up to 10 years in prison on the first count and up to five years on the second. Each charge also carries a potential fine of up to $250,000 and up to three years of supervised release.
